title: Rate limits are denominated in normalised value via the pool's stored_rates, not in raw token units
content:
Every Curve rate-limit charge in this chunk passes through `stored_rates()` first. A...8.1.5 debits `params.amountIn * rates[params.inputIndex] / 1e18`. A...8.2.3 accumulates `valueDeposited += depositAmounts[i] * rates[i]` across all coins before dividing by `1e18`. A...8.3.3 and A...8.3.6 do the same for minimum-withdrawal and actual-withdrawal values.

Raw token amounts are not comparable: a StableSwap pool can mix 6-decimal and 18-decimal assets, and yield-bearing components trade above par. `stored_rates` is the pool's own conversion into a common unit, so multiplying by it converts a heterogeneous vector of token amounts into a single scalar of value.

That scalar is what makes a per-pool limit meaningful. Without normalisation, a limit expressed in token units would mean a different exposure depending on which coin the relayer chose, and governance would have to maintain a separate calibrated limit per asset per pool.

The dependency is worth naming: the limit is only as trustworthy as the pool's reported rates. Grove is reusing the counterparty's accounting to bound its own exposure to that counterparty — acceptable for `stored_rates` and `get_virtual_price`, which are expensive to manipulate and internal to a pool's invariant, but it is the assumption the whole value-denominated limit rests on.
description: Curve deposits, swaps and withdrawals aggregate amount times stored_rates divided by 1e18, letting one limit govern pools whose assets differ in decimals and in exchange rate to the accounting unit.
